title: What Investors Overlooked Before Intel's 127% Run

What Investors Overlooked Before Intel's 127% Run

Intel's year was defined by concrete deals, not just headlines, from Tesla's Terafab choosing its 14A process to Google's multi million TPU order that signaled real foundry demand. For Intel shareholders, the return over the past year was 127.2%, including dividends. If you were deciding whether to buy on 23 October 2025, what exactly did you need to believe about those early contracts and AI bets before the later earnings beats arrived?

Narratives are how investors here put a case on the record, with explicit assumptions about revenue, margins and the multiple. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

Intel has already moved. Pinpoint other ways to investigate the theme among 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

The Argument Intel Investors Were Really Having

The shares cost US$38.16 at the start of the period. Anyone weighing Intel then was really choosing between two structured stories about where the chipmaker might be several years down the road.

The bullish Narrative put Fair Value at US$79, 107% above the start price. It rested on Intel's aggressive roadmap and a cyclical PC rebound, assuming revenue growth of 10.0% with profit margins reaching 22.0% over a 5 year stretch.

The more cautious Narrative set Fair Value at US$25.18, 34% below the start price. It treated Intel's reorganisation and AI focus as helpful but risky, assuming revenue growth of 3.5% and profit margins improving only to 7.8% over 3 years.

NasdaqGS:INTC 1-Year Stock Price Chart
What The Evidence Did To The Intel Argument

Intel's biggest new fact was contract and product traction. Google's multi million TPU order, Terafab's choice of 14A and rising AI CPU demand supported the bullish case that real customers would show up. The reported numbers were less clean. Revenue reached US$16.13b in Q2 2026 versus US$12.86b in Q2 2025, yet the firm still reported a larger loss and a net margin that moved deeper into negative territory.

The lesson for other stocks is simple. When a thesis leans on a profitability fix, treat contract wins and upbeat AI stories as separate from the core test. Check whether net margin, not just sales, is trending toward the level the original Narrative needed.

What Intel's Price Already Bakes In

Intel trades at US$86.96 today, far above where the earlier debate began, while the selected cautious Narrative now puts its Fair Value below that market level. The Narrative credits the turnaround plan and breadth in AI chips but questions how much of that promise can realistically be captured.

A buyer here is effectively assuming Intel converts its roadmap and contracts into durable AI and CPU economics. The open question is how that belief holds up against the Narrative's emphasis on manufacturing execution risk and intense competition in x86 and accelerators.

title: Intel Stock Has Moved an Average of 16% the Day After Its Last 3 Reports. Should You Buy Before the Next One?
detail:
Intel Stock Has Moved an Average of 16% the Day After Its Last 3 Reports. Should You Buy Before the Next One?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 3:37 PM EDT 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) is set to post its third-quarter results after the closing bell on Thursday, Oct. 29. And lately, the trading session after an Intel report has been wild.

The stock dropped 17% the day after Intel's January report, surged 24% after April's, and fell 8% after July's. These three moves average about 16% in one session.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

With shares near $93 as I write, a move that size would mean about $15 a share up or down.

But the quarter Intel had just finished didn't set the direction. The company topped its own financial forecast all three times, and the stock still dropped twice. I think what management said about the coming months mattered more every time.

Image source: Intel.

January and April

In January, Intel posted fourth-quarter 2025 revenue of $13.7 billion and $0.15 in non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, both above the company's own outlook. But management forecast first-quarter 2026 revenue between $11.7 billion and $12.7 billion, with break-even adjusted earnings per share. The midpoint of that revenue range was around 11% under the fourth quarter's total.

"We expect our available supply to be at its lowest level in Q1 before improving in Q2 and beyond," CFO David Zinsner said in the January earnings release.

Shares dropped 17% the next day.

Three months later, the outlook pointed up. Intel's first-quarter revenue of $13.6 billion was $1.4 billion over the midpoint of its forecast. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.29 also beat the break-even level management had guided for, but Zinsner said around 6 cents of that came from a one-time gain.

What's more, Intel forecast second-quarter revenue of $13.8 billion to $14.8 billion, up 2% to 9% over the first quarter. The stock surged 24% on April 24 -- its best day since 1987.

Why did the stock fall in July?

July's report was arguably the best of the three. Second-quarter revenue of $16.1 billion was up 25% from the year before and $1.8 billion above the midpoint of Intel's forecast. Revenue in its data center and AI segment jumped 59% year over year. Adjusted earnings per share landed at $0.42, more than twice the $0.20 management had guided for.

Yet the third-quarter forecast looked flatter. Its revenue midpoint of $16.3 billion sat only about 1% above the second quarter, and Intel guided for adjusted earnings per share of $0.38, down from $0.42. Intel also lifted its 2026 capital spending outlook to over $20 billion, which Zinsner said was "up significantly versus our expectations entering the year."

Intel's foundry unit lost $2.1 billion in a single quarter and pays zero dividend, while GlobalFoundries grows revenue just 6% at a 28% gross margin.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Every time I have extra cash, I buy more Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM). I have stopped apologizing for it. My thesis fits in one sentence. Within five years, TSMC will work like a utility for global computing: a toll road that AI accelerators, smartphone processors and data center chips have to use, and it pays shareholders for every trip.

Courtesy of Intel
Why Every AI Player Pays the Toll

On the third-quarter call, management said it plainly: "all the AI players are working with TSMC." Chips at 7nm and below made up 79% of wafer revenue. Production at 2nm grew from 3% of wafer revenue in Q2 to 8% in Q3. High-performance computing now brings in 68% of revenue. The company also says "demand is still far above our capability to supply today." I look for exactly that in a utility: a broad customer base (534 customers and 12,682 products in 2025) that keeps asking for more capacity than the company can build.

Receipts Behind My Buying

Start with growth. Third-quarter revenue reached $46.72 billion, up 41.2% YoY in USD terms. Management raised its full-year 2026 outlook to around 44% growth. Its Q4 guidance of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion works out to 58% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.

Next comes profitability. Gross margin came in at 66.4%, operating margin at 58.7% and ROE at 45.5%. EPS per ADR of $4.60 beat the $4.46 consensus.
